name: Brazilian tan / spray tan to even skin

lead: A spray tan applies a DHA solution to even out skin tone and give a bronzed look without UV exposure. The color shows within hours, and people use it before events, shoots and competitions.

DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin to produce a brown color rather than acting as a dye. A 2005 review described DHA as the only sunless tanning ingredient approved by the FDA and spray-on products as delivering the formulation evenly for a full-body tan.

paras: The solution is sprayed across the body in a session, and the color develops over hours. It fades over about a week as the outer skin sheds, and people repeat it ahead of events.
The FDA approves DHA for external use only, not for inhalation or mucous membranes. Contact dermatitis and inhalation concerns are reported, and the tan does not protect against UV.

angle.text: A DHA spray tan reacts with the outer skin to give an even bronze color that lasts about a week, with no UV exposure. The color is visible within hours and is used before events, shoots and competitions.

lead: Spray tanning is a sunless tanning method in which a dihydroxyacetone (DHA) solution is applied to the skin to produce a temporary bronze color, used in appearance communities to even out skin tone. DHA reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer rather than acting as a dye [1].

A 2005 review described DHA as the only sunless tanning ingredient approved by the FDA and described spray-on products as delivering the formulation evenly to give a full-body tan without ultraviolet exposure [2].
infobox: DHA approved for external use only

paras: DHA is typically used at about 3 to 5 percent and produces color through a Maillard-type reaction in the outer skin; the color fades as skin sheds over days [1]. Application can be in a booth, by an airbrush technician, or at home [2].

Wikipedia credits Eva Wittgenstein with the 1950s discovery of DHA's skin-coloring effect and lists early products Man-Tan (1959) and Coppertone's QT (1960); automated spray booths spread from the late 1990s [1].

The FDA approves DHA for external application only and not for the eyes, lips, mucous membranes or inhalation, and notes that all-over spray booths can make those exposures hard to avoid [1]. Wikipedia also reports studies on free-radical formation under sun exposure after DHA application and contact dermatitis, and notes that a 2010 European Commission opinion found spray tanning posed no risk but was criticized for relying on unpublished industry-linked studies [1]. A tan from DHA provides no UV protection [1].
No studies found examining spray tans specifically for evening skin tone in looksmaxxing contexts. A 2005 review described the technology and formulations [2].

timeline.event: Man-Tan, an early commercial DHA self-tanner, is released [1].
